Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-09-22](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-09-22).

UN-Habitat reads greenness from space.
For each city it takes satellite imagery, keeps the pixels that stay green for most of the year, and reports them as a share of the city's area.
Trees, shrubs and perennial grass count, and water does not.
The series runs from 1990 to 2020 for every city, so the figure uses that span.

Across 1,110 cities, 65% have a smaller green share than they had in 1990.
UN-Habitat's own global average falls from about 15% to about 10% of city area over the same years.

The regions do not move together.
In East and South-East Asia the median city lost 5.4 percentage points, and 79% of cities lost ground.
Latin America and the Caribbean, Central and South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa each lost about 2 to 4 points at the median.
North America and Europe is the only region whose median city ends where it began, at plus 0.2 points, with its cities split almost evenly between gains and losses.

The extremes are in Africa and Asia.
Kenema and Bo, in Sierra Leone, were three-quarters green in 1990 and are about an eighth green now.
Chengdu fell from 69% to 15%.
At the other end, Stoke-on-Trent went from 8% to 26%, the largest gain in the data.

Some cautions.
A city here is the urban area defined by the Degree of Urbanisation, which can be larger or smaller than the municipality with the same name.
The share says how much of that area is green, not whether parks were lost, so a fall can come from building over fields at the edge as much as from losing trees in the centre.
The data for 2025 exists for only a small number of cities, so it is left out.
The two cities in Oceania outside Australia and New Zealand are too few to draw as a row.
